title: Continuous batcher starvation: post-incident review and remediation plan
creator: Avery Chen
description:
Summary:
During a capacity event on 2026-03-04 we observed repeated tail-latency spikes and temporary throughput loss for a subset of customers using the continuous batcher. The batch formation process entered a starvation state: certain small, long-wait requests were not forming batches due to an interaction between the new fairness heuristic and dynamic sequence-length bucketing. This caused requests to remain pending until a hard timeout (200ms) triggered, producing high p99/p999 latencies and customer errors for latency-sensitive routes.

Impact:
- Duration: ~37 minutes of degraded tail latency across two regions (us-west-2 primary impact).
- Customer impact: medium — several production customers reported timeouts or degraded UX for chat features; no data loss.
- Observable signals: p99 token latency increased 3x, request queue depth grew for prioritized lanes, token throughput dropped ~18% for affected hosts.

Timeline (high level):
- 08:12 — anomaly detection alert: p99 token latency > baseline in us-west-2.
- 08:14 — on-call routed to runtime team; dashboards show persistent pending requests in batch queue.
- 08:22 — mitigations: scaled dedicated pool by +2 nodes; temporary rollback of a scheduling heuristic flagged as suspect.
- 08:29 — measured partial improvement; full recovery after heuristic revert + soft-timeout backstop deployed at 08:49.
- 08:49 — incident declared mitigated; continued monitoring through 09:00.

Root cause (investigation summary):
- A change landed in runtime-1.19 that adjusted continuous-batcher fairness to prefer assembling homogenous-length batches to optimize kernel efficiency. 
- A rare workload pattern (mix of very short interactive requests from PLG customers interleaved with long streaming completions) created an anti-social set of tokens: small requests were deprioritized waiting for same-length mates. 
- The bucket selection algorithm used an aggressive waiting threshold and did not enforce an upper bound on per-request wait time except the global hard timeout.
- Scheduler metric instrumentation did not surface per-customer queue starvation; aggregate queue depth looked normal which delayed detection.

Why this slipped through QA:
- Unit and integration tests validated average latency and throughput but did not exercise mixed-length, low-volume interleaving scenarios at scale.
- No synthetic test covered fairness regressions under cross-tenant low-concurrency mixes.

Mitigations taken during incident:
- Rolled back the new fairness tweak (runtime-1.19 revert) — immediate reduction in pending requests.
- Temporary soft-timeout patch (50ms) added to continuous-batcher to force batch commit when head-of-queue exceeds threshold.
- Scaled up dedicated pool capacity for affected tenants while fixes were being validated.

Longer-term action plan (see action_items):
- Add deterministic unit/integration tests and a chaos job for mixed-length interleaving workloads.
- Enhance metrics: per-tenant pending-time histograms, bucket-level wait-time SLOs, and a fairness health check alert.
- Rework bucket selection to include per-request aging score and soft-commit heuristics before global hard timeout.
